a: Do not be jealous over the wife you hold close
p: Ben Sira warns that suspicion can teach a wife the very thing feared.
b: The "wife of your bosom" (Greek gynaika tou kolpou sou) is the beloved wife, as in Deuteronomy 13:6 and Micah 7:5. The Law had a ritual for a jealous husband who suspected his wife (Numbers 5:11-31). Ben Sira gives practical advice instead: constant jealousy can "teach her an evil lesson," either by giving her the idea, or by teaching her to deceive. Chapter 9 is written to young men about women; it says nothing to women about men, and reflects the society Ben Sira taught in.
orig: Μὴ ζήλου γυναῖκα τοῦ κόλπου σου (mē zēlou gynaika tou kolpou sou)

p: The Hebrew says "to make her tread on your high places," a picture of conquest.
b: The Greek epibēnai autēn epi tēn ischyn sou means "for her to step upon your strength," to master you. The Hebrew in Kahana reads לְהַדְרִיכָהּ עַל בָּמוֹתֶיךָ, "to make her tread on your high places," the picture of a conqueror standing on the heights of a defeated land, as in Deuteronomy 33:29: "you will tread on their high places." Proverbs' Lemuel is told, "Do not hand your strength over to women" (Proverbs 31:3).
orig: ἐπιβῆναι αὐτὴν ἐπὶ τὴν ἰσχύν σου (epibēnai autēn epi tēn ischyn sou)

a: a woman who sells her company
p: The Greek names a Greek kind of paid companion; the Hebrew has Proverbs' "strange woman."
b: The Greek hetairizomenē comes from hetaira, "companion," the word for the educated courtesans of Greek cities, women paid for company and sex. The Hebrew in Kahana has אַל תִּקְרַב אֶל אִשָּׁה זָרָה, "do not go near a strange woman," the figure of Proverbs: "Honey drips from the strange woman's lips" (Proverbs 5:3); "to guard you from the strange woman" (Proverbs 7:5). The grandson used a word his Greek-speaking readers in Egypt would recognize.

a: a woman who plays the harp
p: Women musicians at banquets were often also hired for sex.
b: The Greek psallousa is a woman who plays a stringed instrument; a later hand in Codex Vaticanus wrote above it lyrizousēs, "playing the lyre," as Swete's notes show. At Greek drinking parties such women were hired to entertain, and often to do more. Isaiah mocks Tyre as a forgotten prostitute who takes up her harp and walks the city (Isaiah 23:15-16). The Hebrew in Kahana speaks of "women who play strings" in a separate line.
orig: μετὰ ψαλλούσης μὴ ἐνδελέχιζε (meta psallousēs mē endelechize)

p: The Law made a man who seduced an unmarried girl pay her bride-price.
b: The Greek epitimia are penalties or fines. The Law says, "If a man lures away a virgin who is not promised in marriage and lies with her, he must pay her bride-price and take her as his wife" (Exodus 22:16; see Deuteronomy 22:28-29, fifty shekels of silver). The Hebrew in Kahana, פֶּן תִּוָּקֵש בַּעֲנָשֶׁיהָ, "lest you be snared by her fines," says the same. Job had "cut a covenant with my eyes" not to look at a young girl (Job 31:1), and Jesus taught that a lustful look is already adultery in the heart (Matthew 5:28).
orig: ἐν τοῖς ἐπιτιμίοις αὐτῆς (en tois epitimiois autēs), "in her penalties"

a: you will lose what you inherited
p: Proverbs warns that a man who keeps company with prostitutes wastes his wealth.
b: Proverbs says that a man who keeps company with prostitutes wastes his wealth (Proverbs 29:3). Jesus' story of the lost son has him squander his share, and his brother charges that he spent it on prostitutes (Luke 15:13, 30). The "inheritance" may be the family land, which an Israelite was meant to keep in the family for good (Numbers 36:7-9).

a: Keep your eye off a woman with a lovely figure
p: Ben Sira and Proverbs both locate the start of adultery in the eye.
b: Proverbs warns, "Do not crave her beauty in your heart; / do not let her catch you with her eyelids" (Proverbs 6:25). David's sin began when he saw a beautiful woman bathing (2 Samuel 11:2). The Talmud quotes Ben Sira here in Hebrew: "Turn your eyes from a graceful woman, lest you be caught in her trap... for by the beauty of a beautiful woman many have been destroyed, and mighty are all her slain" (Yevamot 63b; Sanhedrin 100b). Rav Yosef in Sanhedrin 100b names this among the good passages of Ben Sira that may be taught in public. Kahana's bracketed words in 9:10 of his edition come from this Talmud quotation.

t: A married woman, or her husband?
p: The Greek says "a married woman"; the same Hebrew letters can be read "her husband."
b: The Greek hypandros means "under a husband," a married woman. The Hebrew in Kahana has עִם בַּעְלָהּ אַל תִּטְעָם. The letters b-'-l-h can be read be'ulah, "a married woman" (the word of Isaiah 62:4, "Married"), as the Greek took them, or ba'lah, "her husband," as Kahana points them and as the Talmud quotes the line: "Do not turn to her husband to mix wine and strong drink with him" (Yevamot 63b). Either way the warning is against the drinking party that leads to adultery.

t: Sliding to ruin, or to bloodshed
p: The Hebrew adds blood: the angry husband may kill you.
b: The Greek says "in your spirit you may slip into destruction." The Hebrew in Kahana reads וּבְדָמִים תִּטֶּה אֶל שָׁחַת, "and in blood you slide down to the Pit." The "blood" may be the death penalty for adultery (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22) or the revenge of a jealous husband, which Proverbs describes: "jealousy stirs a man's fury, and he will not spare on the day of vengeance" (the thought of Proverbs 6:34). See the variant.
orig: ὀλισθήσῃς εἰς ἀπώλειαν (olisthēsēs eis apōleian), "you slip into destruction"

p: Jesus uses the same comparison of old and new wine.
b: Ben Sira compares a new friend to new wine: it needs time to age before it is good. Jesus said, "Besides, no one who has been drinking the old wants the new. 'The old is good,' he says" (Luke 5:39). Proverbs also prizes the old friend: "Your friend and your father's friend, do not abandon them" (Proverbs 27:10). The Hebrew in Kahana ends, "and old: afterward you may drink it."

a: Do not envy a sinner's glory
p: Ben Sira repeats a frequent warning of the Psalms and Proverbs.
b: "Do not burn up inside over people who do evil; / do not envy those who do wrong" (Psalm 37:1). "Do not let your heart be jealous of sinners; / be jealous instead for the fear of the LORD, all day long" (Proverbs 23:17). Psalm 73 tells of a man who nearly fell because he envied the wicked, until he saw their end (Psalm 73:3, 17). The Greek katastrophē, "overthrow," gives us the word "catastrophe."
orig: ἡ καταστροφὴ αὐτοῦ (hē katastrophē autou), "his overthrow"

a: right up to Hades they will not be acquitted
p: Hades is the Greek word for Sheol, the world of the dead.
b: The Greek hadēs, the god and the world of the dead in Greek religion, was used by the Greek translators for Hebrew she'ol, the place where all the dead go. The Hebrew in Kahana has "death" here: זְכֹר כִּי עַד מַוֶת לֹא יִנָּקֶה, "remember that until death he will not be acquitted." The point is that the wicked will not escape punishment before they die, the view of retribution in this life that runs through the book (11:26). It is not a statement about judgment after death.
orig: ἕως ᾅδου οὐ μὴ δικαιωθῶσιν (heōs hadou ou mē dikaiōthōsin)

a: a man who has power to kill
p: Ben Sira knew the danger of life near a king who could execute at will.
b: In a Hellenistic court, the king or his governor held the power of life and death. Proverbs says, "A king's rage is a messenger of death" (the thought of Proverbs 16:14). Ben Sira's pupils, who might serve such men (8:8), are told to keep their distance, and if they must come near, to make no mistakes. "Walking along the top of city walls," the battlements, is a picture of a place where one wrong step means a fall.

a: the law of the Most High
t: The law of the Most High
p: For Ben Sira, wisdom and the Law of Moses go together.
b: The Greek nomos is "the law," for Ben Sira the Law of Moses. Talk among the wise should be "about the law of the Most High." This joining of wisdom and Torah is one of the book's great themes: in 24:23 Wisdom is identified with "the book of the covenant of the Most High God," and in 39:1 the scribe gives himself to the study of the law. Psalm 1 blesses the one who murmurs God's law day and night (Psalm 1:2). Compare Mishnah Avot's saying that when two sit together and words of Torah pass between them, the Presence of God is with them.

a: let the fear of the Lord be what you boast in
t: Boasting in the fear of the Lord
p: Jeremiah says the only right boast is in knowing the LORD.
b: The Greek kauchēma is a boast, a ground of pride. Jeremiah says, "If anyone is to boast, let it be in this alone: / that he shows insight and knows me" (Jeremiah 9:24), and Paul applies it: "Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord" (1 Corinthians 1:31). The phrase "the fear of the Lord" (Greek phobos Kyriou) is Proverbs' great theme (Proverbs 1:7), and Ben Sira uses it more than any other book outside Proverbs; it returns in 10:19-24.
orig: ἐν φόβῳ Κυρίου ἔστω τὸ καύχημά σου (en phobō Kyriou estō to kauchēma sou)

a: A loudmouth is feared in his city
p: Proverbs and James warn of the reckless tongue.
b: The Greek anēr glōssōdēs, "a tongue-ful man," is the same word as in 8:3. Proverbs says the one who opens his lips wide comes to ruin (Proverbs 13:3), and James calls the tongue "a small member" that can set a whole forest on fire (James 3:5). The Hebrew in Kahana adds "and one who carries a burden on his mouth will be hated."
